text:
Ask most people what melanin is and you will hear something about a tan, or about skin colour. That is true as far as it goes, but I think it sells one of the body's cleverer systems short, because melanin is really a shield for your DNA.

Melanin is a pigment, that is, a natural colouring, made by melanocytes, the pigment-making cells in the skin. It is not melatonin, the sleep hormone, despite the similar name. In this animation from HHMI BioInteractive, narrated by Penn State anthropologist Nina Jablonski, who studies how human skin colour evolved, you can watch the shield being built:

• Inside each melanocyte are tiny packages called melanosomes, which are the factories that make melanin.
• Those melanosomes travel along the melanocyte's long arms and are handed over to keratinocytes, the main cells of the skin's surface.
• Some of them settle into a cap around the nucleus, the part of the cell that holds its DNA.
• There the melanin absorbs ultraviolet energy, so less of it reaches the nucleus, and especially the DNA.

That raises a question I had not thought to ask. If melanocytes build the shield for every other skin cell, what protects the melanocytes themselves? Years of sun leave small changes in their own DNA, called mutations, which you can think of as scars in each cell's instruction manual.

A study published this year in Nature Cell Biology offers a surprising answer. A UCSF-led team grew 297 single melanocytes from the outer skin of 31 people into small colonies and read their DNA. Even in sun-exposed skin, a group of them carried very few mutations, and those cells were smaller, less branched and more like stem cells, that is, cells that can make new cells. Mapping the skin by gene activity placed cells with that low-mutation profile mostly in hair follicles, the tiny pockets each hair grows from, so the authors propose that follicles act as a sun-sheltered reserve that restocks the skin after sun damage.

That reserve is their proposal rather than something the study proved, and because this is a lab study of cells and tissue, it says nothing about tanning, sunscreen or skin health, but it is a striking picture all the same.

So the next time someone calls melanin "just what makes a tan", you will know it is a shield built for your DNA, possibly with a quiet reserve of its makers tucked away at the roots of your hairs.

text:
THE LESSON OF THE GALLOWS — JUSTICE, DETERRENCE, AND FORT HOOD

Justice must be served. But must the world watch?

On November 5, 2009, Nidal Hasan murdered 13 Americans and wounded 32 others at Fort Hood, Texas.

His execution by firing squad is scheduled for December 3, 2026. The Pentagon intends to livestream it.

Secretary Pete Hegseth wants the world to understand that murdering American soldiers carries the gravest consequences.

I understand that reasoning. Accountability matters. Deterrence matters. Justice for the victims and their families matters.

But history offers a warning.

During the 1800s, public hangings were intended to discourage crime, demonstrate government authority, and reassure citizens that justice was being served.

Thousands gathered to watch. Vendors sold food. Crowds cheered. Executions often became public entertainment.

Did they prevent crime?

Perhaps some. But history provides little reliable evidence that making executions public significantly reduced criminal behavior.

By 1868, Britain had abolished public hangings. Capital punishment continued, but the spectacle ended.

Now consider Fort Hood.

We are no longer talking about thousands gathering around a gallows. We are talking about potentially millions watching an execution broadcast worldwide, recorded permanently, and shared endlessly.

And we must recognize something particularly troubling about terrorism.

Some extremists do not fear death. They welcome martyrdom. They seek attention, recognition, and the opportunity to inspire others.

Could livestreaming this execution unintentionally accomplish exactly what we hope to prevent?

I don’t know. But the question deserves serious consideration.

Justice and spectacle are not the same thing.

We can support the lawful punishment of a convicted mass murderer without turning his final moments into worldwide entertainment.

We can demonstrate American strength without giving a terrorist one final international audience.

Most importantly, we must never allow the execution itself to overshadow the 13 innocent Americans whose lives were stolen.

Their sacrifice deserves remembrance. Their families deserve justice. Our military deserves protection.

The objective must be to discourage the next terrorist, not simply punish the last one.

The greatest demonstration of American strength is not how publicly we carry out punishment, but how consistently we uphold justice.

Let the world remember the victims of Fort Hood.

Not the spectacle of their murderer’s death.

text:
I'm for Standard Time, but a little Texas History surround Quanah, Texas, if anyone likes history. 

My mother was born there...kinda irrelevant but she was. 

Now for the history part. 

Quanah, Texas was named for Quanah Parker who was the last Comanche chief, specifically of the Quahadi. 

Quanah Parker was half-white and took his mother's name when he moved to the reservation when he surrendered at Fort Sill in 1875. His grave is there. The headstone reads, "The Last Chief of the Comanches". 

Quanah Parker was born to Peta Nocona and Cynthia Ann Parker (Comanche name is Naduah) in 1845. Nocona was a war leader of the Quahadi. Naduah was a blonde-haired and blue-eyed woman around 19 or 20 years old, who once went by the name Cynthia Ann Parker until she was taken by the Comanches in 1836 from her family's fort near Groesbeck, TX. 

You can visit Old Fort Parker. We used to go on field trips there. 

Fort Parker was her family's fort- parents, grandparents, siblings, etc. One day they were playing just outside the gates and saw some dust stirring up, meaning someone was coming on horseback. 

The kids went inside the fort and the men stood outside. Most of the men were gone that day, about a mile away in the fields. Her grandfather, her uncle Benjamin, and her father Silas spoke to the 100 or so Comanche who came with a white flag. 

The Comanche asked for food, but with so few currently at the Fort, the Elder Parker had decided to decline. The Elder Parker and Silas headed back into the Fort to try and get the woman and children out of the back gate. Benjamin went back out the front and was killed by a lance. The Comanche came through the gate before Silas could get it closed and he, along with the Elder Parker were killed. Their headstones are at the Fort. 

Around 20 people were able to escape, but Cynthia Ann (around 9 years old) and several of her cousins and brothers were taken for trading or ransom. Everyone was ransomed alive, except Cynthia Ann. 

The Comanche never offered to ransom her. They took her in and treated her as their own. She had adoptive parents who raised her. 

Her uncle never gave up looking for her. She was found once and refused to leave. She was married and had children. Comanche life was all she knew. Her Comanche parents had also said they would rather die than ransom her. 

Eventually, she was found again at the Battle of Pease River. This is located near Crowell in west Texas. My grandparents live there along with some cousins. She was taken by rangers during the battle, along with her infant daughter Topsannah, also known as Prairie Flower, and returned to her family. 

Cynthia Ann was now Naduah, mother to Chief Quanah. She tried to escape several times to return to her Comanche family. She refused to adopt the Anglo life and would sleep on the floor. 

Unfortunately, Topsannah, having never been exposed, got the flu and died from pneumonia as a baby. Naduah, Cynthia Ann, then grieved to death. 

There is a marker just outside of Crowell, between it and the ghost town of Margaret, that tells of the Battle of Pease River and Naduah's capture by the rangers. 

I also thought it was an interesting and sad story for all...and that I got to stand in both places she was taken- one by the Comanches as Cynthia Ann and one by the rangers as Naduah, mother of the Great Chief Quanah. 

Pictured: Chief Quanah Parker and Naduah (Cynthia Ann) and Topsannah (Prairie Flower)

text:
Frankie Wills (pictured) gets KOd in the 1st-round by undefeated (23-0) on October 9, 1944 at Metropolitan Opera House in Philadelphia.

Wills, born Francesco Guido, was among many Italian-American boxers in the first half of the 20th century that fought under anglicized, or Irish, names. He went 49-26-6 with 8 KO wins from 1936-46.

From Philly Boxing History:

The Met was opened in 1908 as the Philadelphia Opera House. Designed and built by theater impresario Oscar Hammerstein, the venue was the largest of its kind at the time with a seating capacity of more than 4,000 for opera events. It's grand opening came on November 17, 1908 with a performance of Bizet's Carmen. Two years later in 1910, the venue was sold to the Metropolitan Opera of New York, and renamed the Metropolitan Opera House. It operated as an opera house through 1922, and around 1920, also began showing movies. In the late 1930s, boxing promoter Jimmy Toppi purchased the building and converted it into a boxing venue. As a fight site, the Met offered 193 boxing events from 1939 to 1954, with a seating capacity for boxing around 5,500. This made the Met one of the biggest indoor boxing arenas in the city during its time. Only Convention Hall and the Arena had more space for indoor boxing.

The very first boxing show featured Norristown's Tony Cisco in an six-round main event against Wicky Harkins of Germantown. Cisco won the bout by decision to launch the Met's boxing life. The promoter of the show was former light heavyweight champion Tommy Loughran, who was the house promoter through 1940, staging 11 shows in all. Then the venue went dark in 1941, 1942 and 1943.
In 1944, the Met came back to life. With Jimmy Toppi as the new house promoter, the Met ran boxing events continuously for the next ten years. The first event in this new run, was on October 9, 1944, and featured rising teenage welterweight sensation Billy Arnold. Known as "The New Joe Louis", Arnold was on a tear. His first round KO of Frankie Wills at the Met stretched his career-staring unbeaten streak to 25-0. That streak would extend to 31 straight bouts. This first fight of the Met's second chapter drew approximately 5,200 fan, and still stands as the venue's biggest boxing box office record.

Over the year, the Met would host countless local boxing stars, including Joey Giardello, Percy Bassett, Wesley Mouzon, George Benton, Gil Turner, Eddie Giosa, Tommy Forte, Johnny Forte, Bobby Green, Jimmy Tygh, Gene Burton, Dorsey Lay, Santa Bucca, Jetson Arnold, Toothpick Brown, Ellis Phillips, Johnny Walker, Freddie Sammons, George LaRover, Otis Graham, Billy Thompson, Honeychile Johnson, Gil Turner, Carmen Bartolomeo, Marvin Edelman, Dan Bucceroni, as well as Kid Gavilan, Ike Williams, Lew Jenkins, Johnny Saxton, and many others.

At its peak, the Met offered 34 shows in 1946 and 36 shows in 1947. Activity dipped some during the 1950s, but there were excellent fights, often high profile cross-town rivalries, every year through the remainder of its run.

The final show at the Met came on November 18, 1954, and was promoted by Jimmy Riggio. In the main event, veteran Gil Turner stopped the rising Charley Scott in eight rounds. After this event, the Met halted its boxing life and eventually closed completely.
However, unlike other great Philly boxing venues, the Met's story ends on a much more upbeat note. Instead of being torn down and totally forgotten, the Met survived through the years and eventually received a multi-million dollar renovation in 2018. Purchased by Live Nation, a national concert promoter, the Met returned with a varied schedule of events, including boxing.

On February 23, 2019, Hard Hitting Promotions (Manny Rivera and Will Ruiz) staged the first boxing event at the Met in more than 64 years. The eight-round main event was a clash of two rising, undefeated local lightweights, Steven Ortiz and Jeremy Cuevas. Ortiz won the decision and with it earned the PA State Lightweight Title.

text:
There is a kind of western that still wants you to leave the theater believing a man can be mean and still be the remedy. The Hateful Eight is not that western. It is the western that locks the remedy in the same room as the disease and then refuses to tell you which is which, because the answer is that there is no which. Quentin Tarantino’s 2015 chamber piece, set in the Wyoming winter after the Civil War and released as both a ordinary feature and a resurrected roadshow, stands out from the field not by being bloodier than its cousins, though it is bloodier, and not by being talkier, though it is talkier than almost anything that still calls itself a western, but by withdrawing the last courtesy the genre usually grants. It will not give you a good guy. Not a stained good guy. Not a good guy who does one ugly thing and is forgiven by the frame. Not a good guy hiding inside a uniform, a bounty paper, a sheriff’s claim, a lady’s name, or a letter used to fool people. The picture’s claim on legend is that it treats moral comfort as a lie the audience has been trained to expect, and then spends nearly three hours proving the lie cannot survive a blizzard.

What you are supposed to learn begins with the shape of the trap, not with a catalogue of corpses. A stagecoach is pushing toward Red Rock with a prisoner who is meant to hang. A storm closes the road. The only shelter is a haberdashery in the mountains, one room, one stove, one bar, one door the snow intends to keep shut. Fate, in this film, is not a judge. Fate is weather. It does not sort the righteous from the wicked, because the righteous are not on the coach and they are not waiting by the fire. It simply seals a set of bad people, operating at different levels of bad and for clashing motives, inside a box where every sentence can become a weapon and every cup of coffee can become a verdict. That is why the movie feels unique even among mysteries and even among Tarantino’s own work. Reservoir Dogs had thieves. This has a cross section of the country’s unfinished war, bounty law, outlaw loyalty, and plain meanness, all of them convinced the other man’s evil is the only evil in the room. The takeaway is not that civilization fails when good people are outnumbered. The takeaway is colder. Civilization, in this telling, was never waiting outside the door. The door only decides which hatredes get to finish their argument.

Call the inhabitants what they are, and do not let presentation talk you out of it. John Ruth, called the Hangman, is a bounty hunter who will not kill his prisoner on the trail because he wants the pleasure and the payment of a legal rope. That preference is not mercy. It is a narrower cruelty with paperwork. Daisy Domergue is the prisoner, foul mouthed, already bloodied, and no less a killer for being chained to a man who hits her. Major Marquis Warren is the other bounty hunter, a black Union veteran whose corpses are worth money and whose survival has required him to be as ruthless as the country that tried to erase him. Ruthlessness in his case has a history. It does not have an exemption. Chris Mannix is the son of a Confederate marauder who claims he is the new sheriff of Red Rock, a man whose past is raid and murder and whose present is a badge he may or may not actually hold. The men already at the haberdashery present themselves as a Mexican caretaker, an English hangman, a quiet cowboy writing a letter home, and an old Confederate general. The story later peels those presentations. Under them are members of a gang whose motive is to free Daisy before Red Rock can hang her. Motive does not baptize them. A rescue conducted by poison, ambush, and lies is still a killing floor. The general’s age does not soften the massacre he ordered. The hangman’s manners do not soften the noose he sells. Even the people who actually belong to Minnie’s Haberdashery, the ones the gang has already removed, are not offered to you as innocents the film forgot to mourn. Warren tells the room what used to hang over that bar. The sign said no dogs or Mexicans allowed. Minnie hung it the day she opened. It stayed up until she decided dogs could come in. Mexicans remained the line she would not cross. She liked just about everybody, he says, but she sure did not like Mexicans, and she would not have left the most precious thing she owned in a Mexican’s hands. The house itself was built on a slur. The people who kept it carried that slur as policy. When the gang takes the house, one racism displaces another. The walls do not become clean.

The only narrow exception the story leaves you is the stagecoach drivers, the men whose work is the road and the horses rather than the bounty, the noose, the raid, or the gang. Everyone else who matters is bad. The differences are level and motive, not kind. One wants a legal hanging. One wants a payday on corpses. One wants a town he can police in the image of his father’s war. One wants a sister, or a partner, pulled off the gallows. One wants the old cause avenged in memory. One wants the old cause paid in blood. They clash because the storm has annulled the distance that normally lets such people pass one another on a trail. A western usually lets the good gunfighter ride away from the men he is not. This western cancels the ride. That cancellation is the masterpiece. You are not watching a hero discover who the villain is. You are watching villains of unequal wattage discover that the room is too small for all their certainties.

Hold the two bounty hunters and Mannix in the same thought, because the film does. Warren states the position without apology. The only time black folks are safe is when white folks are disarmed. He has used a letter to fool people into exactly that disarmament, a prop that lowers white hands and buys him a seat he would otherwise be denied. The letter is not a relic of virtue in his pocket. It is a tool. Mannix states the mirror position with the same certainty. White folks are safe when black men are scared. Hear those two sentences as one doctrine turned around. Safety, for each man, is not law, not neighborliness, not even the temporary truce of a shared stove. Safety is the other race placed at a disadvantage, either by empty hands or by fear. The picture refuses the audience’s wish to grade these lines. It does not award Warren the moral win because his history is the history of the enslaved and the betrayed, and it does not award Mannix the win because he wears the future badge of Red Rock. Both men are describing a peace that is only the other man’s helplessness. That is the lesson you are supposed to carry out of the coach and into the haberdashery. Racism in this film is not a costume worn by the obvious villains so the complicated men can look cleaner. It is the shared weather inside the room. Ruth carries it. Warren carries it. Mannix carries it. The sign over Minnie’s bar carried it. The gang that replaced Minnie carries its own version, aimed wherever the plan requires. Level differs. The flaw does not.

What the closed battle teaches, once the coffee is poured and the suspicions start to walk, is that a fight among the guilty does not become justice by process of elimination. Ruth wants his hanging. The gang wants its rescue. Warren wants to know who is lying and to be paid for the men he has already killed. Mannix wants to arrive in Red Rock as something more than his father’s son. The old general wants the past to remain proud. None of these wants cancels the others into goodness. When the lies break, they break into gunfire, poison, and a floor that belongs to whoever is still able to hold a weapon. You live by the gun, you die by the gun. The film does not offer that as a slogan painted on a saloon. It offers it as the only consistent law the room obeys. The Hangman’s pride in bringing prisoners in alive does not keep him alive. The bounty hunter’s skill with a pistol does not promote him to redeemer. The gang’s ambush does not become noble because Daisy is the one in chains. The sheriff’s claim does not sanctify the last men standing. Whoever reaches for the gun to settle a motive has already agreed to the settlement the gun provides, which is not a verdict. It is an ending. The audience that came for a western mystery learns the mystery, and then learns that solving it changes nothing about the moral floor. The impostors were impostors. The house was already a racist house. The men who exposed the impostors were not thereby cleansed. Identification is not absolution.

This is why the film stands out among westerns, among chamber thrillers, and among movies that advertise moral complication while quietly keeping one character hireable as the audience’s proxy. Most films in the field still smuggle a good guy. They may dirty him. They may make him kill. They may make the town worse than he is. They still point the camera so that his survival feels like a correction. The Hateful Eight points the camera at a table and lets every face at the table be a reason not to trust the table. Charm does not save them. Wit does not save them. A tragic backstory does not save them. Being right about one liar does not save them. The cultural icon status of the picture comes from that refusal, repeated until it becomes the style. People return to it not for a plot they can summarize into heroes and turns, but for the sensation of being denied the usual exit. It became a legend because it is quotable and vicious and formally grand, yes, and also because it is one of the rare popular films that will not let you outsource your conscience to a protagonist. You watch it to practice suspicion against your own relief. Whenever the frame starts to make one man look like the necessary man, the next scene asks what he is necessary for, and the answer is never innocence.

The must watch case is therefore not that the movie is exciting, though the tension is a kind of slow strangling, and not that the dialogue is pleasurable, though the dialogue is the real ammunition. The must watch case is that the lesson cannot be received secondhand. You have to sit in the room long enough to feel yourself trying to pick a side, and long enough to notice that every side you pick asks you to ignore a sign, a doctrine, a blow, or a pile of bodies that side has already agreed to. Warren’s disarmament theory and Mannix’s fear theory are the clearest version of the trap, because they sound, to opposite listeners, like hard earned wisdom. The film sets them side by side so the rhyme can be heard. One man wants the other race harmless. The other man wants the other race afraid. Both call the result safety. A country that accepts either sentence has not ended its war. It has only changed which body is required to stay vulnerable. That is the takeaway the plot exists to teach. The blizzard, the coach, the false names, the coffee, the guns, all of it is machinery for forcing that rhyme into the open.

Behind the picture, the making matches the severity of the argument. Tarantino shot it in Ultra Panavision 70, a format barely used since the roadshow epics of the nineteen fifties and sixties, with an image wide enough to make a single room feel like a landscape and a landscape feel like a sentence that will not end. The roadshow version ran with an overture, an intermission, and a program, in about a hundred theaters fitted again with 70mm projectors, a deliberate throwback that treated the audience’s endurance as part of the design. Ennio Morricone, who had not scored a western in decades and had never before written a full original score for Tarantino, composed from the script and a conversation, and the score won him the Academy Award, the competitive Oscar that had eluded the composer of the most famous western music ever written. The exteriors were built on a high mesa near Telluride and shot in cold that the cast described as freezing, with snow groomed again and again so the nineteenth century would not show the tracks of modern machines. Jennifer Jason Leigh spent long days actually chained to Kurt Russell, a disturbed dance partnership that kept Daisy’s bondage from becoming a prop the actress could set down between takes. The production went over its original budget. A script had already been stolen and leaked before shooting, and the film itself leaked online before release, so the secrecy of a mystery movie was broken in public and the movie still worked, because its secret was never only who was lying. Its secret was that no one’s truth was going to save the room. Samuel L. Jackson, Kurt Russell, Jennifer Jason Leigh, Walton Goggins, Demián Bichir, Tim Roth, Michael Madsen, Bruce Dern: a company of actors asked to keep every character intelligent, funny, and unforgivable at the same time. That is the last fact worth keeping beside the lesson. The movie was hard to shoot because the argument was hard to fake. You cannot photograph a moral vacuum with charming shortcuts. You have to build the cabin, freeze the road, chain the prisoner, hire the composer of the old myth, and then let the myth die of its own guns.

So the legend is not that The Hateful Eight is the western with the best twist. The legend is that it is the western that finishes the thought other westerns keep postponing. There are no good guys in the haberdashery, whatever uniform, chain, badge, accent, or letter they carry, and the people who kept the place before the gang arrived had already nailed their racism to the wall in a sign that admitted dogs before it would admit Mexicans. The bounty hunters and Mannix do not escape that indictment by being better shots or better talkers. One says black men are safe only when white men are disarmed. One says white people are safe only when black men are scared. Those are the same race position. The storm does not care which one you prefer. It only guarantees they will have to say it in earshot of each other, and then live by the gun until the gun finishes them. Watch it for that. Leave it with that. Anything softer is a story this movie already refused to tell.

Northern Kentucky MAGA donor Eric Deters is accusing U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle of trying to get him to quietly pay off a $100,000 American Express bill days before her Senate confirmation.

The Wall Street Journal reported the alleged Signal texts from July 3, 2025… six days before her July 9 hearing. According to messages Deters provided, she wrote: “It won’t show up anywhere if you wire money to American Express that’s all that will show,” then “Honey please I need you to get this done for me today,” with a prayer-hands emoji and an Amex payment PDF.

Deters calls it quid pro quo. He says she offered to be his “Trump ride or die” and help get his tax and legal problems in front of administration officials if he sent the money. He says he didn’t pay —didn’t have the cash, told her it would end his marriage and has also admitted that if he’d had it, he would have sent it. He claims he’d already paid her about $300,000 over the years and gotten nothing back.

Guilfoyle’s lawyer disputes the texts and says she was owed money for event appearances. CBS reports White House officials were told the messages were authentic, and that some Trump aides were not pleased. Marco Rubio has declined to address it.

Deters is a suspended Northern Kentucky attorney who ran for governor in 2023 and Congress in 2024 and says he put more than $1 million into Trump. He is now saying she should lose the ambassadorship.

text:
India’s Russian oil imports just hit their lowest level since March 2022. Bloomberg tanker tracking shows the four-week average through October 4 collapsed to 310,000 barrels per day.

Indian refiners are also cutting purchases scheduled for November delivery.

The share of Russian crude in India’s import mix fell from 56% in July to roughly 35% in September, according to Kpler, a structural shift away from the Kremlin’s war budget.

The pricing mechanism broke. Russian Urals from Baltic ports is now offered at a premium above $10 per barrel to Dated Brent.

The discount era that made Russian crude irresistible to Indian buyers is over. Urals is now priced near Middle Eastern grades, and Indian companies are returning to suppliers in the Persian Gulf.

China is the reason. Beijing is buying more Russian oil because its access to Iranian crude is shrinking.

That demand is pushing Urals prices up and making Gulf suppliers competitive again on shorter routes with lower freight costs.

The analysis from @Deepstate_UA lays out the sequence clearly. Bloomberg sources say economics, not Washington pressure, is driving the shift.

The threat of US tariffs already forced Indian refiners to cut purchases earlier, but New Delhi never ordered them to reduce Russian imports.

India and China remain the largest buyers of Russian crude. The destination of many cargoes is still decided mid-voyage.

But the price signal now works against Moscow, and the Kremlin has no way to spin it.

text:
Jonathan Keeperman (@L0m3z) gave a speech at the Nat Con conference, and I posted a crude reaction to it. He asked me politely if I would explain myself.  Here is my response:

Jonathan, thank you for your gracious response to my rather ungracious characterization of your speech. I appreciate your civility. Let me explain what provoked my reaction.

I agree with your central premise. Today's political climate calls on us to justify the American-Israeli alliance in terms of American national interests. But after calling for a hardheaded accounting of costs and benefits, you never actually perform one. Instead, you offer a selective account of the grievances that some American nationalists harbor toward Israel and its supporters. At several points, you toggle almost imperceptibly between describing those grievances impartially to validating them, without acknowledging the toggle.

You came to Jerusalem while the United States and Israel were engaged in a war against Iran. American and Israeli forces have fought alongside one another on an extraordinary scale. Both countries have committed military power and made great sacrifices in a struggle against a common enemy. Yet you barely acknowledge the war, let alone consider what it reveals about the value of the alliance.

Surely that experience belongs at the center of any serious discussion of what America gains from Israel.

There is also a question of elementary respect. You came to a country at war to explain why Americans are growing weary of its demands on their attention and resources. You found time to discuss the immigration preferences of liberal American Jews and the political sins of the ADL, but not the soldiers fighting, the lives being lost, or the sacrifices being made in a common struggle. Whatever your intentions, that is a failure to recognize the gravity of the occasion.

And it is inseparable from the larger failure of your analysis. You tell us that Israel receives $3.8 billion annually in American assistance. But what does the United States receive in return? What is the value of Israeli intelligence, military power, technological innovation, and cooperation against common adversaries? What role does Israel play in America's competition with Iran, China, and Russia? What would it cost the United States to replace the capabilities and regional influence that the alliance provides?

These questions are the beginning of the prudential calculation you call for but never undertake. More importantly, what would happen if Washington weakened the relationship to the point that Israel concluded it could no longer rely on the United States?

No sane Israeli wants that outcome. But national survival may force Israel to contemplate it in the coming years. Israel would not simply disappear as a strategic actor. It would become a more independent one, making decisions about war, peace, deterrence, and relations with other powers with less regard for American preferences.

American support does not give Washington control over Israeli decisions, but it does help keep Israeli military power integrated into an American-led regional order. That is an asset with considerable strategic value. If Israel became a de facto free agent, Washington might save money and escape some immediate obligations, but it would also surrender influence over one of the most formidable military powers in the Middle East.

And Israel would not be operating in a vacuum. China and Russia would have opportunities to exploit the resulting realignment. Iran would have opportunities of its own. The regional order would change, and not necessarily to America's advantage.

Perhaps you believe this would be a good bargain. But you never consider the possibility, much less calculate its costs. You call for realism while leaving the most consequential strategic questions unexamined.

Your treatment of the American right is similarly selective. You emphasize the growing skepticism of younger conservatives, but you never mention that Donald Trump, the dominant figure in the nationalist movement you describe, has taken American military cooperation with Israel to unprecedented levels.

Trump recognized Jerusalem as Israel's capital, recognized Israeli sovereignty over the Golan Heights, withdrew from the Iran nuclear agreement, and brokered the Abraham Accords. In his second term, he went much further, committing American military power to a joint war against Iran. How does his record fit your account of national conservatism? Why does the behavior of the nationalist president receive less attention than the attitudes of young nationalists? Is Trump an anomaly? Does he misunderstand the movement he leads? Or might his support for Israel reflect a nationalist assessment of American interests fundamentally different from the one you describe? These questions are indispensable to your argument. Yet you don't address them. 

I am also troubled by your treatment of antisemitism. You correctly observe that accusations of antisemitism no longer carry the political force they once did. But the declining effectiveness of an accusation tells us nothing about the reality or seriousness of the phenomenon it describes.

There has been a conspicuous resurgence of antisemitic rhetoric in parts of the American right. Influential voices have promoted the idea that American foreign policy is controlled by Jews or manipulated on Israel's behalf. Such claims encourage Americans to interpret strategic decisions through theories of sinister manipulation rather than through an examination of American interests. 

Antisemitism, therefore, is not simply a problem for Jews. It is a problem for American national security, political judgment, and national cohesion. It also offers opportunities to foreign adversaries seeking to weaken the United States from within.

Yet in a speech devoted to explaining declining support for Israel on the right, you give remarkably little attention to the role that antisemitic agitation has played in producing that decline. Instead, you place considerable responsibility on Israel's American defenders. You blame neoconservatives for opposing Trump, liberal Jews for supporting immigration, and even the ADL for antagonizing populists.

Your reference to the ADL is particularly strange. What do the immigration preferences of liberal American Jews have to do with the strategic value of America's alliance with Israel? The ADL is an American Jewish organization, not an arm of the Israeli government. American Jews are predominantly liberal. They disagree with national conservatives on many domestic questions. So what?

Even if every criticism you make of the ADL were justified, what do they have to do with the value of Israel as an American ally? Nothing, unless one assumes that Israel bears responsibility for the political behavior of American Jews. That is precisely the kind of collective attribution that ought to be examined critically, not casually incorporated into an explanation of why Americans are turning against Israel.

The same problem appears in your treatment of America's wars in the Middle East. You say they are closely associated with Israeli interests. Associated by whom? Which wars? Which interests? And how accurately does that association explain actual American decisions?

You leave those questions unanswered. Instead, you point to deeply tendentious interpretations of American foreign policy -- ones often advanced by antisemites such as Tucker Carlson -- as though they were established facts. Arguments frequently employed by Israel's worst antagonists enter your speech disguised as an objective description of American attitudes.

This brings me to a broader problem with your method. You present yourself as a relatively detached observer of Israel and an informed observer of the American right. But throughout the speech, you alternate between describing the attitudes of nationalists and adopting their explanations for those attitudes. Reporting that some conservatives blame Israel for America's Middle Eastern wars is one thing. Treating that blame as an adequate explanation of their alienation is another.

Political attitudes do not develop in a vacuum. Personalities, institutions, and campaigns of persuasion shape them. Yet your account assigns considerable agency to Israel's defenders, whose conduct supposedly alienated the nationalist right, while giving remarkably little attention to the people on the right actively encouraging hostility toward Israel and Jews based on the most vile lies. You thus present the consequences of an ideological struggle as though they were an impersonal historical development to which Israelis must accommodate themselves.

Finally, there is something peculiar about the posture of the speech itself. You begin by explaining that Israel has never occupied a central place in your thinking and that you make no claim to expertise about it. Fair enough. But you then proceed to deliver sweeping judgments about the future of the alliance and the political adjustments Israelis must make.

There is nothing wrong with an outsider offering uncomfortable observations. But the authority of those observations depends on their accuracy, not on the speaker's professed detachment. You conclude by imagining an Israel that Americans "do not have to think about." 

But the Middle East will not cease to matter to the United States simply because Americans grow tired of thinking about Israel. Iran will not abandon its ambitions. China and Russia will not relinquish their interests. And Israel's enemies will not stop threatening it because American voters would prefer to concentrate on domestic affairs.

The question is whether America is better positioned to manage those challenges with Israel as a close ally or with Israel acting increasingly on its own. That is the prudential question you say would should address. It is also the question your speech conspicuously avoids.

I don't know you. I have no basis for judging your intentions. I accept that you may regard your speech as a candid warning delivered in good faith. But whatever your intentions, its effect is to give a veneer of dispassionate analysis to a series of highly dubious claims about Israel, Jews, and American foreign policy. That is what I objected to. And it is why I reacted so strongly.

Washington Democrats created a new income tax and are now discovering that collecting it is harder than passing it.
Washington’s New Income Tax Already Has Problems
Washington Democrats are still trying to figure out how their brand-new income tax is supposed to work—and they’re already discovering that collecting it is a lot more complicated than passing it.

The state’s new 9.9% tax currently applies to households earning $1 million or more, but lawmakers have already floated lowering that threshold to $750,000, $500,000 or even $250,000. So taxpayers have plenty of reason to wonder where the line will eventually be drawn.
Now the state’s income-tax advisory group has uncovered another problem: there’s no “safe harbor” for people who unexpectedly become subject to the tax.

In other words, someone could earn under the $1 million threshold one year, cross it the next, pay the full tax they owe—and still face a penalty because they didn’t make enough estimated payments during the year.

Rep. Noel Frame, D-Seattle, essentially acknowledged that lawmakers didn’t think through that scenario when they wrote the law. As she put it, “we solved the problem for just the taxing and effect initially, but we didn’t think about it” for someone who becomes subject to the tax later.

That’s quite the admission for a tax that is supposed to bring in billions of dollars.

And the problems don’t stop there. The state is also trying to determine how to track and collect the tax from nonresidents whose income is connected to Washington through complicated partnership structures. The Department of Revenue had already warned lawmakers during the legislative session that determining who actually owes the tax would be difficult.

So Washington Democrats created a complicated new tax, the Department of Revenue warned them about implementation problems, and now an advisory group is working through basic questions about how taxpayers are supposed to comply.

And remember: this is the current $1 million threshold. Some Democrats have already discussed lowering it dramatically.

Maybe before Washington creates an even bigger tax base, lawmakers should figure out how to make the tax they already passed actually work.

Voters will get their say on Initiative 645 this November, which would repeal the new income tax. It would also add another chapter to Washington voters’ long history of rejecting a state income tax at the ballot box. Read more at The Center Square.

More Taxes, More Spending, Less Accountability

Washington local governments have discovered a remarkably simple solution to their transportation and budget problems: ask taxpayers for more money.

According to the Washington Policy Center, cities and counties already have broad authority to raise transportation taxes and fees through Transportation Benefit Districts, yet local governments continue heading to Olympia looking for even more state funding. Meanwhile, proposals in Bellevue and Seattle raise questions about whether new transportation taxes will actually improve transportation.
Bellevue is considering a 0.1% sales-tax increase plus $20–$40 in vehicle fees, potentially pushing its sales-tax rate to 10.5%. But according to the Washington Policy Center, less than 20% of the proposed funding would go toward vehicle mobility and no more than 8% toward street preservation. Much of the money would go toward vague categories such as “neighborhood mobility,” bike and pedestrian projects and “major projects.”
Seattle wants to go even further, proposing a 0.3% sales-tax increase expected to generate $138 million annually. Much of that money would subsidize Metro bus service, continue operating the Seattle Streetcar and provide free ORCA passes to low-income residents.

Meanwhile, 35% of Seattle’s streets are reportedly in poor or very poor condition.

And then there’s King County.

On Tuesday, the County Council approved another 0.01% sales-tax increase without asking voters, with the money going into the Department of Community and Human Services for shelter and rental assistance. There isn’t even a detailed spending plan yet—the council will decide how to distribute the money later.

That’s especially interesting because DCHS is already under scrutiny for how it has handled existing taxpayer dollars.

An independent review found $690,617 in questioned costs across 16 community organizations connected to DCHS programs, including unsupported cash withdrawals, questionable stipends and potentially altered documents. The county’s Ombuds office concluded that waste, fraud or abuse likely occurred in some cases.

And on the same day the council approved the new tax, it appointed an Inspector General to investigate fraud and recover misspent funds.

So the pattern is becoming pretty familiar: Washington governments want more revenue first and accountability later.

Bellevue wants higher taxes despite questions about how much will actually improve roads and vehicle mobility. Seattle wants another $138 million while a third of its streets are in poor or very poor condition. King County wants another tax while one of its departments is under investigation for questionable spending.

The Washington Policy Center argues that transportation taxes should come with clearer priorities, cost-effectiveness requirements and accountability for whether the money actually improves the transportation system.

That’s not exactly a radical concept.

Before Washington asks taxpayers for another dollar, maybe government should demonstrate what happened to the dollars it already collected. Read more at the Washington Policy Center and Seattle Red.

Thinking about the Ft. Hood shooter tonight.
After Benedict Arnold met with a British major named John Andre to discuss what the Brits would offer in exchange for information, the fact of their meeting leaked and both men scurried to get away.  Arnold managed to make good his escape.  But Major Andre had originally intended to leave the area via the British warship HMS Vulture. and that ship had already been spotted and forced to withdraw under heavy shore battery fire.
As an alternative, Arnold gave Andre some civilian clothes and a fake passport under the name "John Anderson."   Arnold also insisted that Andre hide the maps and other documents he'd given him in his boots.
Andre's escape went horribly wrong when he met a trio of American militiamen, one of whom happened to be wearing a discarded Hessian coat, and he mistook them for loyalists.  He was captured, tried, and sentenced to death.
He requested of General Washington that, since he was a military man, he be given a military firing squad.  But Washington said no.  The general declared that Andre was captured while dressed as a spy, so he would face the indignity of being hanged.  Thus illustrating for me that firing squad is a more honorable death than hanging.
So I say, save the ammunition and get a rope,

@WeTheBrandon put Robert Barnes on under a title the lawyer has already been willing to carry. This is not the Trump Americans voted for. What the term has delivered is a running war with Iran, carriers timed to the far side of a midterm, a Venezuela oil claim counted in the tens of billions of barrels, and a White House that will not take the Insurrection Act off the table before the vote. MARYLAND GREEN PARTY CANDIDATE BLASTS MOORE AND COX, CITES UMBC POLL AS EVIDENCE OF VOTER DISSATISFACTION.

Andy Ellis, the Maryland Green Party candidate for governor, says the latest UMBC poll shows voters are frustrated with both major parties and looking for alternatives.

Ellis criticized the gubernatorial debate between Democratic Gov. Wes Moore and Republican Dan Cox as “boring” and “uninspiring,” arguing that neither candidate offers meaningful change.

Citing the poll, Ellis highlighted several findings:

• 60% of likely voters support allowing unaffiliated voters to participate in primary elections.

• More than 70% of unaffiliated and younger voters support opening primaries.

• Nearly 90% of likely voters, according to Ellis, identify money in politics and declining trust in government as major threats to democracy.

Ellis also called for banning data centers in Maryland, accusing both parties of failing to address residents’ concerns.

“Both parties are finally waking up to this anger, and both parties come up short on solutions,” Ellis said.

Ellis and running mate Owen Silverman Andrews are campaigning on open primaries, opposition to data centers and reducing corporate influence in government.

text:
The United States Department of Defense announced that the impending execution of convicted Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan will be broadcast live to the public. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth confirmed the unprecedented decision regarding the high profile military case, emphasizing that officials intend to ensure maximum visibility for the event. Hasan, a former Army major and psychiatrist, was convicted in connection with the tragic 2009 mass shooting at the Texas military base that left thirteen individuals dead and dozens of others wounded. The scheduled execution, set to be carried out by a firing squad, marks a historic departure from modern correctional norms, as the U.S. military has not executed a service member by firing squad in decades.

During a media appearance, Hegseth addressed the arrangements bluntly, stating that authorities would make certain people are able to watch the proceedings and that the event would be handled publicly. Pentagon officials subsequently clarified these remarks, confirming that a livestream will be arranged and that additional logistical specifics will be released as the execution date approaches. The decision immediately ignited nationwide legal, ethical, and political debates regarding transparency, the nature of state sponsored capital punishment, and the appropriateness of broadcasting such an event to a mass audience.

Legal scholars and death penalty experts have offered sharply contrasting viewpoints on the move. Some analysts suggest that livestreaming capital punishment could introduce a stark layer of absolute transparency, forcing the public to confront the harsh realities of the death penalty firsthand. Conversely, critics and civil liberties advocates argue that turning a state execution into a public broadcast serves more as a political spectacle than a measure of justice, raising serious questions surrounding human dignity, legal precedents, and the potential psychological impacts on viewers. As the scheduled date draws near, defense attorneys and legal experts continue to evaluate potential challenges that could alter the timeline or execution method, leaving the unprecedented plan under intense national scrutiny.

"And so, in a fashion that was all too familiar to anyone who remembered the history of the French anti-war Socialists of an carlier time, people around the world rushed to suggest ways in which the apparent mass pathologies were anything but pathologies, and terror was reasonable and explicable and perhaps even admirable. Some people convinced themselves that Islamist ideology was not Islamist ideology. Hamas, to them, was not Hamas, and the goal of those suicide bombers was a moderate and plausible two-state partition-a solution worthy of the United Nations, with terror as a mere pressure tactic, like a labor strike. Some people convinced themselves, on the other hand, that Israel had no right to exist, and Islamist ideology was fair and reasonable on this issue, and suicide terror advanced a just cause.
Some people-a far greater number-recognized that suicide terror-was tactically unproductive, and that suicide was suicide. And yet, suicide terror vented authentic, therefore commendable, emotions. Suicide terror, in this interpretation, sang the song of Palestinians who could no longer endure life without a state of their own. 
Some people suggested that Israel's religious fanatics, the ultra-right, in seizing new parcels of land for settlement colonies, had driven masses of Palestinians out of their minds, especially young people, who now preferred to die. And the suicide terrorists were, in fact, crazy, but their enemies and not their leaders and their own doctrines were to blame.
There was, in short, an idea that each new act of murder and suicide testified to how oppressive were the Israelis. Palestinian terror, in this view, was the measure of Israeli guilt. The more grotesque the terror, the deeper the guilt. And, if unfathomable motives appeared to drive the suicide bombers forward, the oppressiveness of Israel was likewise deemed to be, by logical inference, unfathomable-a bottomless oppression, which had given rise to the maximum of violence, which is suicide murder.
The commuter buses, the pizza parlors, the discos, the hotel dining rooms, the bustling sidewalks--these exploded into random carnage.
And, with every new atrocity, the search was on to find ever larger accusations to place at Israel's feet. These accusations spun variations on a single theme. It was the idea that Zionism was something more than a program of national self-determination for the Jews, more than a simple and straightforward doctrine of Jewish self-defense. Zionism was, on the contrary, racism-a program of hatred and contempt for other people. And, with this idea established, a declension of tropes and images marched steadily forward within the arguments of the new Palestinian sympathizers. The comparison between Israel and the old white Republic of South Africa from the days of apartheid marked only the first of those tropes. That was an easy comparison to make, a natural, for anyone who imagined (as most people seemed to do) that Israels non-European Jews did not exist, and that Israel's European Jews were not principally refugees but were, instead, colonial settlers, and that Zionism, like apartheid, was a doctrine of contempt for the non-Europeans.
Yet not even this trope sufficed to explain the suicide terror. Yet not even this trope sufficed to explain the suicide terror. In South Africa during the worst days of white racism, the anti-apartheid resistance movement engaged in all kinds of violence and even some acts of random terror, though never as a large-scale policy; yet the South African resisters managed not to slip into the lowest rung of nihilist despair. How to explain that, by contrast, the Palestinians had done just that? Palestinian nihilism could only mean that Palestinian sufferings were, in some important respect, worse, and by far, than South Africa's in the past. The South African analogy therefore yielded to a grimmer and angrier trope, which was Nazism. Israel became,  in the rhetoric of its accusers, a Nazi entity-a state so utterly devoted to evil, so far beyond the bounds of human decency as to make suicide murder a comprehensible reaction on the part of its victims."

O Glorious Prince of the heavenly host, Saint Michael the Archangel, defend us in the battle and fearful warfare that we are waging against the principalities and powers, against the rulers of this world of darkness, against the evil spirits. Come thou to the assistance of men, whom Almighty God created immortal, making them in His own image and likeness and redeeming them at a great price from the tyranny of Satan. text:
Grok 

No. That post is false. It is a recycled version of a made-up story that started circulating on X around October 4, 2026.

The account claims Jane Fonda said she feels “betrayed” by Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass and Governor Gavin Newsom because they denied a permit to rebuild her Malibu mansion after the fires, and that the state offered her $1.3 million — about half the appraisal — so the land could become a sanctuary for the “California Sandpiper.” She supposedly turned the offer down, and they then made the property worthless.

None of that is supported:

- Jane Fonda does not live in a Malibu mansion that burned. August 2026 reporting still places her in a Century City home bought in 2017 for about $5.45 million and valued around $6 million. She is not on the lists of celebrities whose homes were destroyed in the January 2025 Palisades Fire (Paris Hilton, Mel Gibson, and others are).
- There is no news report, city record, or statement from Fonda, Los Angeles, Malibu, or the state about a denied rebuild permit or a $1.3 million (or $1.5 million, in the earlier version) buyout of her land.
- The quotes attributed to her do not appear anywhere outside these X posts. The earlier version, from @DorothyStangle, used slightly different wording and a $1.5 million figure. This post just rewrote the same claim.
- “California Sandpiper” is not a species name used in California coastal protections. Shorebird fights in Malibu involve birds such as the western snowy plover.
- In May 2026 she endorsed Karen Bass for reelection. That is the opposite of the “betrayed” story.

Real disputes over Malibu and Palisades rebuild rules exist — slow permits, SB 9 duplex limits in burn zones, CEQA fights — but this incident and these quotes do not.

text:
🇧🇷 AFTER HOURS CITY REVIEW: FORTALEZA, BRAZIL

Fortaleza was once considered one of Brazil’s better mongering destinations, but recent reports suggest the traditional P4P scene has declined significantly. The city still has plenty to offer, particularly for guys interested in meeting regular women.

📍 Meireles/Beira-Mar is the best base. The waterfront is clean, modern and lined with restaurants, bars and exercise facilities. Praia de Iracema offers livelier nightlife, particularly around Ponte dos Ingleses. Praia do Futuro has impressive beach clubs, but the surrounding area receives mixed reviews. Check hotel and Airbnb guest policies before booking.

🌃 The Scene: Fortaleza isn’t what it used to be. Veterans report fewer streetwalkers, closed establishments and a shrinking traditional P4P scene. Zipi Bar remains operational, but recent visitors describe a heavily male-dominated atmosphere. One November 2025 report counted approximately 45 men and 10 women by 1 AM. Armazen is reportedly permanently closed.

👠 P4P: Activity remains around Iracema and Beira-Mar, though considerably reduced. Budget puteiros around Rua 24 de Maio and Rua Sena Madureira still operate, but reviews describe inconsistent quality and poor conditions. Monsenhor Tabosa 111 received a serious warning following a dispute over session time and alleged threats involving police.

📱 Regular Dating: Arguably Fortaleza’s biggest strength. Multiple visitors report friendly, flirtatious women and considerable success with Bumble and Tinder. One traveler returned twice within a month after meeting several non-professional women. Intermediate Spanish can help, although Portuguese or a translation app is preferable.

🍺 Nightlife: Hoots receives positive reviews for its weekend crowds and live music. Praia de Iracema, particularly near the Pirate Bar and Ponte dos Ingleses, is another favorite. Beira-Mar is generally quieter and more conservative. Several visitors found the nightlife considerably more promising than the daytime beach scene.

💃 Swinging: Revolution Swing Club received a positive April 2025 report from a visitor attending with a Tinder date. He described a busy venue and adventurous atmosphere, although information about the broader swinging scene remains limited.

🏝️ Beyond Fortaleza: Canoa Quebrada offers a smaller coastal nightlife scene concentrated around Bar Caverna, Vips and Bar the Tia. However, recent reports suggest declining activity and fewer women than in previous years. It’s more of a beach getaway than a serious mongering destination.

💰 Costs: Fortaleza remains cheaper than Rio, particularly for accommodation and dining, but isn’t exceptionally inexpensive. One recent report listed two beers at Zipi Bar for R$60. Longer stays in apartments can offer better value, provided guest restrictions aren’t an issue.

🏆 Verdict: Fortaleza is now a better destination for conventional dating, beach culture and nightlife than traditional P4P. The old mongering scene has clearly lost momentum, but the city’s attractive waterfront, active dating apps and lively local bars still make it worth considering. Travelers expecting another Pattaya or Angeles City will likely be disappointed.

AHA Rating: 6/10

Best for: Regular dating, dating apps, beachfront nightlife & longer stays.

Weaknesses: Declining P4P scene, limited quality venues, male-heavy bars & accommodation guest restrictions.

Best area to stay: Meireles / Beira-Mar 🇧🇷

OPENAI IS BACK IN THE PRICE. SOFTBANK $SFTBY LEFT 6,310 YEN:

SoftBank Group SFTBY at $17.90, -$1.90 / -9.60% on Thursday.

That is -$1.72 / -8.77% from the $19.62 in the quoted post. The 6,310 yen that post said the shares had returned to did not hold. At 10:12am Tokyo time on Friday, on a 15-minute delay, SoftBank was at 5,714 yen, -326 yen / -5.40% from Thursday's close. That print is not a close.

The verdict: the quoted post moved this week's risk off OpenAI and onto a Delaware trial over chip-design royalties. The price did not wait for the jury. A Financial Times report on how OpenAI counts revenue landed on Thursday, and a Friday morning note in Tokyo names that report. No verdict has been reported. Court in Wilmington has not started its Friday session.

Wednesday was not the down day. Wednesday's regular close was $19.80, +$0.18 / +0.92% from the $19.62 in that post. Thursday was.

Tokyo since that 6,310 yen close:

- Thursday's close: 6,040 yen, -270 yen / -4.28%.
- From 6,310 yen to Friday's 10:12am print: -596 yen / -9.45%.

Thursday's yen drop was wider than Japan's benchmark.

- Nikkei 225 (Japan): 69,042.11, -993.60 points / -1.42% at Thursday's close.

SoftBank pulled the index down by more than any other name. Its contribution was -218.44 points. That was just over a fifth of the drop.

Friday morning, at the same hour as the SoftBank print, is not a close either.

- Nikkei 225 (Japan): 68,227.73, -814.38 points / -1.18% from Thursday's close, at 10:11am Tokyo time.

SoftBank's morning drop is wider than the index. The gap belongs to the stock.

Arm Holdings (ARM) at $275.29, -$19.08 / -6.48% on Thursday.

Arm designs chip blueprints and collects a royalty, a fee on each chip built from them. SoftBank owns most of Arm. Thursday in New York was a wider percent drop for SoftBank than for Arm, and wider than Thursday's finished session in Tokyo.

- Arm since the Tuesday close in that post: -9.0%.

That is nearly the same percent as SoftBank's US-traded shares. Thursday's single session is not. Arm is on none of the six Len5 watchlists. A down day with no ruling is the opposite of the months-long climb the Momentum Len5 follows.

Qualcomm (QCOM) at $176.01, -$1.11 / -0.63% on Thursday.

Qualcomm brought the case and fell far less than Arm. It is on none of the six Len5 watchlists: an unfinished lawsuit is not a months-long climb, a discount, or cash paid out to owners.

- VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) at $607.27, -$17.76 / -2.84% on Thursday.

The fund holds the large US-listed chip stocks and has no business of its own, so no Len5 applies. SoftBank's US-traded drop was more than three times that percent.

The report is a counting method, not lost sales. Annualized revenue is the pace of sales, stretched over a year.

- Financial Times, Thursday: OpenAI told investors that pace was approaching $50B at the end of September, against about $70B in earlier reports, including the FT's own.
- The gap, on the FT's account: investors were lining OpenAI up with Anthropic, a private rival that counts cloud-partner sales differently. OpenAI declined to comment.
- CNBC put the earlier figure near $68B, including those partner sales.
- Third-quarter growth, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC: 77% for the whole business, and 107% for sales to companies.

The lower headline did not come with a report that sales had shrunk.

Fisco, via Kabutan at 10:19am Tokyo time, said SoftBank was falling sharply as an OpenAI investor on that report. SoftBank has not filed it.

The court has moved less than the shares. Reuters corrected its Monday story: the chart the quoted post called an 1,800% royalty jump, from one blueprint to the next, is an 18,500% jump in the corrected account. It is still the lawyer's chart, not a finding. Electronics Weekly reported that on Wednesday Qualcomm offered to pay up to 5% above the best rate Arm gives any other customer for the next blueprint, and Arm refused. The last scheduled jury day is Friday, October 9, before Judge Maryellen Noreika in Wilmington. That session has not started. No date has been reported for her separate ruling on whether Qualcomm can stop paying.

Market value is the share price times the shares that exist. The comparison in the quoted post still points the same way.

- Arm, all the shares, at Thursday's close: $294B.
- SoftBank's stake, Arm's annual report as of May 21: 922,733,999 shares, 86.4%.
- That stake at Thursday's Arm close: about $254B.
- SoftBank's own market value: 34.50 trillion yen, about $218.5B at 157.86 yen per dollar.

The stake is still about $35.5B larger than the whole company. On that math, the market is pricing everything else SoftBank owns, OpenAI included, at less than zero. Friday morning is marking the shares down on OpenAI's revenue definition anyway.

SoftBank is still on none of the six Len5 watchlists. The Deep-Value & Special-Situations Len5 wants a price well below a cautious value, or a dated event that turns a stake into cash. The trial can change what Arm earns. The report can change what people think a private company is worth. Neither pays SoftBank cash. What would put SoftBank on the Deep-Value & Special-Situations Len5: a sale or listing that turns part of the OpenAI or Arm stake into cash near SoftBank's own value. What would put SoftBank on the Momentum Len5: a climb that lasts for months after the November 10 report, or after a royalty ruling.

- 3:00pm Tokyo time, 2:00am ET: the regular close. The 5,714 yen print can still move.
- Friday in Wilmington: the last scheduled day of testimony. Tokyo will already be closed.

Public posts about SoftBank over the past day were light, and the few that took a side leaned down. That is the conversation, not the holdings.

What would make Friday the revenue report through the Tokyo close: SoftBank still down more than the Nikkei at 3pm, and no new figure from OpenAI. What would hand the next move to the court: a ruling on whether the royalty pause stays in the case. The risk is treating a counting method and an unfinished lawsuit as one event.

Friday in Tokyo is reacting to how OpenAI's sales are counted. Friday in Wilmington has not started. Only the second can change what Arm charges per chip.

Not investment advice.

SoftBank Group (SFTBY) at $19.62, -$0.69 / -3.40% on Tuesday.

That is -$0.96 / -4.7% from the quoted post's $20.58. In Tokyo, where most of SoftBank's shares trade, three sessions since that post ended on the same 6,310 yen close it printed. The verdict: the quoted post's read has held, because the stock has closed none of the gap to SoftBank's own count. But this week's risk is not OpenAI's price tag. It is Arm, the chip designer SoftBank owns nearly 90% of, now in court against one of its largest customers over what it may charge.

SoftBank in Tokyo since Friday:

- Monday: 6,497 yen, +187 / +2.96%.
- Tuesday: 6,295 yen, -202 / -3.11%.
- Wednesday: 6,310 yen, +15 / +0.24%.

- Nikkei 225 (Japan): 70,036, -648 points / -0.92% at Wednesday's close.

Since Friday's close, Japan's benchmark has gained 2.5%. SoftBank has gained nothing.

Tuesday erased Monday's gain. The Nikkei rose 1.05% that day, so the drop was SoftBank's own. It came the morning after a trial over Arm's royalties opened in Delaware, and after Arm slipped about 1.5% in New York.

The US line has now fallen in step with Tokyo. On Friday it barely moved, because Arm jumped in New York after Tokyo had closed. Measured from Thursday's close, the last before the final OpenAI payment was announced:

- Tokyo: -5.8%.
- US line: -5.5%.

Now the trial.

Arm Holdings (ARM) at $302.56, -$0.34 / -0.11% on Tuesday, and $294.31 premarket, -$8.25 / -2.73% from that close.

Qualcomm (QCOM) at $181.03, +$0.24 / +0.13% on Tuesday.

Qualcomm took Arm to trial on Monday in federal court in Wilmington, Delaware, Reuters reported. Its claims:

- Arm withheld chip-testing tools it owed Qualcomm under contract.
- Arm leaked to the press its 2024 threat to cancel Qualcomm's license.
- The prize: Qualcomm wants to stop paying Arm royalties, the fee Arm collects on each chip built with its designs, for up to five years. Reuters puts that at potentially billions of dollars.

Arm denies breaking the contract and calls the harm Qualcomm claims speculative. Underneath is a fight over price. In a related hearing the judge decides alone, over whether Arm has bargained in good faith on its next licensing terms, Qualcomm's lawyer kept returning to a chart showing Arm seeking an 1,800% increase in royalties from one version of its chip blueprint to the next. Arm's lawyer asked Qualcomm chief executive Cristiano Amon whether a 2013 deal, priced for small phone chips, means Qualcomm pays for five processor cores on a 288-core data-center chip and is "getting 283 for free." Amon: "I don't see it that way."

For scale, Arm's whole revenue in the year to March was $4.92B, on $904M of profit. Billions over five years from one customer would weigh on both.

Two deciders, two clocks. A jury is hearing Qualcomm's claims in a trial scheduled for five days. Separately, Judge Maryellen Noreika is weighing whether to throw out the contract term that would let Qualcomm stop paying, and no date for that ruling has been reported.

Why SoftBank's owners should care comes down to one comparison, at Tuesday's closes:

- Arm's market value, what all its shares were worth: $323B.
- SoftBank's market value: $227B.

SoftBank owns nearly 90% of Arm, so that stake alone was worth more than the whole company. In effect, the market is giving SoftBank no credit for anything it owns beyond Arm, OpenAI included. Arm shares also back the $25B loan the quoted post noted. A ruling that lets Qualcomm stop paying would land on the asset that carries both.

Arm is on none of the six Len5es: at about 311 times its past year's profit, the price runs far ahead of the profit. Qualcomm is on none of them either; at about 21 times its past year's profit, the discount the value styles wait for is missing.

SoftBank is still a pick on none of the six Len5es, and this week did not move that. The nearest remains Deep-Value & Special-Situations, which hunts a price well below a cautious value of the business, or a dated event that changes the math. The trial is a dated event, but not that kind: it can change what Arm earns, not turn any stake into cash. What would put SoftBank on the Deep-Value & Special-Situations Len5 is unchanged: a sale or listing that turns part of the OpenAI or Arm stakes into cash near SoftBank's own value.

Next: the jury trial runs through this week if it keeps to schedule, and the judge's ruling has no date. After that, the quoted post's dates stand: Arm's results, tentatively November 4, and SoftBank's on November 10. The key risk is the order: a ruling on Arm's royalties can arrive before SoftBank publishes its next count of what it owns.

Three Tokyo sessions brought SoftBank back to the yen it started at. What can move it now is not what OpenAI is worth on paper but what Arm may charge for each chip, and a judge in Wilmington holds part of that answer.

text:
Here are my three takeaways from tonight's 5-2 Montreal Canadiens loss to the Nashville Predators, brought to you by Snap Bar Sportif in Rigaud and Biggs in Hudson.

1- Canadiens face adversity early

This was one of those games the Canadiens had absolutely no business losing.

Montreal was the better team for large stretches, generated plenty of scoring opportunities, and yet somehow came away empty-handed in the standings.

They ran into a red-hot Juuse Saros and had a couple of unfortunate breaks along the way. But don't start playing the world's smallest violin for the Canadiens. Games like this are going to happen over the course of an 84-game season. It's just particularly frustrating when you lose one that looked like it should have been the free space on the bingo card.

The difficult start to the season also continues for Mike Matheson, who had put together a solid performance until late in the third period. He mishandled a puck in a play reminiscent of his costly mistake in Pittsburgh, then compounded the error by taking a penalty while trying to recover.

Nashville capitalized on the ensuing power play, scoring what turned out to be the game-winning goal while Matheson watched helplessly from the penalty box.

It's an unfortunate sequence for a player who had otherwise been having a good night, but it's another reminder of how quickly an individual mistake can undo a lot of good work.

And the schedule isn't about to offer Montreal much relief.

After hosting the Detroit Red Wings on Saturday, the Canadiens face the Buffalo Sabres twice and the Washington Capitals next week.

With two consecutive losses on home ice and a less-than-ideal start to the season, the Canadiens are facing a little adversity earlier than anticipated. It's hardly time to panic, but Martin St. Louis shouldn't have much trouble getting his team's attention.

2- Stop breaking up Caufield-Suzuki-Slafkovsky

The number one line works. It has worked, and more often than not, it will continue to work. Enough with the constant tinkering.

Juraj Slafkovsky bounced back with a better performance than Tuesday night against Carolina, Nick Suzuki found the back of the net, and Cole Caufield generated several quality opportunities but couldn't convert.

When Montreal drafted Slafkovsky, this was always the vision. The player himself even called his shot shortly after the draft: "They can use me on that line because they are small and I am big."

It's understandable, and even reasonable, to want more balance throughout the lineup. The injury to Ivan Demidov certainly threw a wrench into those plans, and there's no question the Canadiens would benefit from spreading out their offensive firepower down the road.

But that balance has to come from somewhere other than breaking up one of the best lines in hockey. Montreal has spent years trying to establish a legitimate top line. Now that they have one, they should stop looking for reasons to separate it.

That doesn't mean the line is going to produce every night, but there's a difference between a combination that isn't working and one that simply isn't converting its chances.

3- With his spot in doubt, Xhekaj plays with confidence

Adam Engstrom made his season debut, with Jayden Struble becoming the odd man out. Martin St. Louis has already acknowledged the logjam of capable NHL defensemen on his roster, and with everyone healthy, somebody is inevitably going to be left watching.

Engstrom had a respectable first outing, but one of the more encouraging individual performances on the blue line came from Arber Xhekaj.

Xhekaj played with confidence, particularly with the puck on his stick. He made several good decisions, looked comfortable moving the puck, and found himself involved in the play offensively more often than usual.

Obviously, nobody is expecting Xhekaj to become an offensive dynamo. That's not why he's in the lineup. But seeing him make confident, decisive plays with the puck is a positive development, especially for a player whose consistency has been questioned.

You can't help but wonder whether the increased competition is providing a little extra motivation. With Struble waiting for another opportunity and Engstrom now in the mix, Xhekaj knows he could be the next player to "miss his turn."

It wasn't a performance that will overshadow the disappointing result, nor does one solid game guarantee his place in the lineup. But on a night when the Canadiens had plenty of reasons to be frustrated, Xhekaj gave the coaching staff something positive to build on.

Thought
“Kings chapter 5” usually means one of two different chapters. Here is what each covers.

1 Kings 5 — Solomon prepares to build the temple
After David’s death, Hiram king of Tyre (a longtime friend of David) sends envoys to Solomon. Solomon replies that David could not build a house for the Lord because of wars on every side, but God has now given Israel rest. Solomon intends to build that house, as God promised David, and asks Hiram for cedar and cypress from Lebanon. Sidonian workers are skilled at cutting timber; Solomon will pay their wages.

Hiram agrees, praises God for giving David a wise son, and arranges for the timber to be floated by sea as rafts to a place Solomon chooses. In return, Solomon supplies Hiram’s household with wheat and oil year by year. The two kings make a treaty, and the Lord gives Solomon wisdom as promised.

Solomon then raises a labor force from Israel: 30,000 men sent to Lebanon in shifts (10,000 a month, one month there and two at home), under Adoniram. He also has 70,000 burden-bearers and 80,000 stonecutters in the hills, plus 3,300 overseers. They quarry large, costly stones for the temple foundation, and Solomon’s and Hiram’s builders, with the Gebalites, prepare the timber and stone.

(Note: some Catholic editions number the chapter differently and begin 1 Kings 5 with Solomon’s wealth and daily provisions, which Protestant Bibles place at the end of chapter 4.)

2 Kings 5 — Naaman healed of leprosy
Naaman, commander of the army of the king of Aram (Syria), is a great and honored man because the Lord had given Aram victory through him—but he has leprosy. A captive Israelite girl serving Naaman’s wife says the prophet in Samaria could cure him. The king of Aram sends Naaman with a letter, silver, gold, and clothing to the king of Israel.

Israel’s king tears his clothes, thinking Aram is looking for a pretext for war. Elisha hears of it and tells the king to send Naaman to him. Naaman arrives with horses and chariots. Elisha does not come out; he sends a messenger: wash seven times in the Jordan and you will be clean. Naaman is angry—he expected a dramatic ritual and prefers the rivers of Damascus—but his servants persuade him to try the simple command. He dips seven times; his flesh is restored like that of a young child.

Naaman returns, confesses that there is no God in all the earth except in Israel, and offers a gift. Elisha refuses it. Naaman asks for two mule-loads of earth so he can sacrifice only to the Lord, and for pardon when he must accompany his master into the temple of Rimmon. Elisha sends him away in peace.

Gehazi, Elisha’s servant, runs after Naaman, lies that visitors have come, and takes silver and clothing. Elisha confronts him. Gehazi leaves with Naaman’s leprosy, his skin white as Snow
